questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic with a draining lesion on his forearm. Gram stain of the purulent drainage shows purple-staining spherical bacteria arranged in irregular, grape-like clusters. Which of the following genera do these organisms most likely belong to?

explanation.summary: Staphylococci are gram-positive cocci that characteristically clump in grape-like clusters.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococci stain purple because they are gram positive, they are spherical, and they tend to cluster together like grapes rather than forming pairs or chains. This appearance in pus is the first clue to the genus. Because all staphylococcal species look identical on Gram stain, biochemical testing is needed to identify the species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clostridium species are gram-positive, spore-forming rods rather than cocci in clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corynebacterium species are gram-positive bacilli and would appear as purple rods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neisseria species are gram negative, stain pink, and appear as diplococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococci are also gram-positive cocci, but they are arranged in chains rather than clusters.

questions.stem: A laboratory isolates gram-positive cocci from a wound culture and must determine whether the organisms belong to the genus Staphylococcus rather than Streptococcus or Enterococcus. Which of the following tests is most useful for this distinction?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are catalase positive, which separates them from Streptococcus and Enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococci produce catalase, the enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, so mixing a colony with hydrogen peroxide produces visible bubbles. Streptococcus and Enterococcus species do not produce catalase. A positive catalase test therefore places a gram-positive coccus in the genus Staphylococcus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All staphylococci grow in the presence of bile salts, so this result does not sort organisms by genus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulase separates S. aureus from the other staphylococci; it does not sort the genus from streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannitol fermentation on salt agar identifies S. aureus within the staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Novobiocin sensitivity is used to pick out S. saprophyticus among coagulase-negative staphylococci.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man reports a swollen, red bump about 1 inch across on his calf that he thought was a spider bite. There is a pale tan peak at the center that has drained thick exudate, the area is tender and hot, faint red streaking extends proximally, and the inguinal lymph nodes are palpable. Which of the following best describes the lesion and its most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An abscess caused by S. aureus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bullous impetigo caused by S. aureus

explanation.summary: A localized pocket of pus in soft tissue is an abscess, most commonly caused by S. aureus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abscesses are collections of pus in tissues, organs, or other spaces, and S. aureus is the most common cause. They often begin at a trivial break in the skin such as a scratch or an infected hair follicle that was too minor to notice. Management is incision and drainage, with antibiotic coverage that includes MRSA when there is surrounding spread.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bullous impetigo produces fluid-filled blisters on an erythematous base rather than a deep pus collection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. saprophyticus colonizes the urogenital tract and causes urinary infection, not soft tissue abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folliculitis is confined to a hair follicle and appears as a small tender pustule, not a draining pocket of pus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and would not present as a superficial draining skin nodule.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old sexually active woman has 2 days of burning with urination, urinary frequency, and suprapubic pain. She recently returned from her honeymoon. Urine culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative, and resistant to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: A coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus causing cystitis in a young woman is S. saprophyticus.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. saprophyticus is part of the normal urogenital flora and is the staphylococcus that causes urinary tract infections and cystitis in sexually active young women. Among the staphylococci it is uniquely resistant to novobiocin, and like other coagulase-negative species it fails to clot plasma. Risk factors include sexual activity, a short urethra, and open cuts or sores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecalis is catalase negative and does not form grape-like clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a gram-negative rod and would not appear as gram-positive cocci in clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. aureus is coagulase positive, so the negative coagulase test excludes it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. epidermidis is coagulase negative but is sensitive rather than resistant to novobiocin.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 58-year-old woman with a tunneled central venous catheter develops low-grade fevers. Two blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative, and sensitive to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: S. epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and the classic pathogen of indwelling catheters.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. epidermidis is a commensal of the skin that is coagulase negative and novobiocin sensitive. It readily colonizes foreign bodies such as central venous catheters and Foley catheters and causes severe endogenous infection in immunosuppressed patients. Its tendency to adhere to plastic surfaces makes catheter-related bloodstream infection its signature presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecalis is catalase negative, so it would not be identified as a staphylococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. aureus clots plasma in the coagulase test and is therefore ruled out.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and is associated with urinary rather than catheter infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus agalactiae is catalase negative and grows in chains rather than clusters.

questions.stem: An isolate of gram-positive cocci in clusters is streaked onto mannitol salt agar. After incubation, the medium surrounding the colonies has turned from red to yellow. This color change is a direct result of which of the following properties of the isolate?

explanation.summary: Yellowing of mannitol salt agar means the organism ferments mannitol, as S. aureus does.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mannitol salt agar contains mannitol plus a pH indicator. S. aureus ferments mannitol and the acid produced turns the agar yellow. Staphylococci that do not ferment mannitol grow as small pink or red colonies and leave the color of the medium unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-hemolysis is clearing of red blood cells on blood agar, a different medium entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Novobiocin resistance is read as growth up to an antibiotic disk rather than as a color change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catalase is detected by bubbling when colonies are mixed with hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coagulase production is detected by clotting plasma in a tube, not by a color change in agar.

questions.stem: Mannitol salt agar is used as a selective medium for gram-positive organisms such as staphylococci. Which component of the medium provides this selectivity?

explanation.summary: Mannitol salt agar for Staphylococcus is selective because of its 7.5% sodium chloride.
explanation.whyCorrect: For Staphylococcus, mannitol salt agar usually contains 7.5% sodium chloride. Most bacteria cannot tolerate that salt concentration, so the medium selects for salt-tolerant gram-positive organisms. The mannitol and pH indicator then differentiate S. aureus, which ferments mannitol and turns the agar yellow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sheep blood is the component of blood agar and is used to read hemolysis patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Novobiocin is applied as a disk in a separate test used to identify S. saprophyticus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bile salts are not the selective agent here, and all staphylococci grow in their presence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydrogen peroxide is the reagent for the catalase test, not a component of the medium.

questions.stem: A catalase-positive, gram-positive coccus that grows in clusters is plated on blood agar and produces colonies surrounded by a clear zone of complete red blood cell lysis. Which of the following additional laboratory results is expected for this isolate?

explanation.summary: Of the main staphylococci, only S. aureus is beta-hemolytic, and only S. aureus is coagulase positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Culturing on blood agar reveals complete lysis of red blood cells by S. aureus, leaving a pale or clear zone around the colonies. S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are nonhemolytic. Because S. aureus is also the only one of the three that produces coagulase, a beta-hemolytic staphylococcus should clot plasma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, are nonhemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. aureus ferments mannitol, which is why it turns mannitol salt agar yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is sensitive to novobiocin; only S. saprophyticus is resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All staphylococci are resistant to bile salts and grow in their presence.

questions.stem: A student is trying to tell apart S. aureus, S. epidermidis, and S. saprophyticus in the laboratory. Which of the following results is identical for all three species and therefore cannot be used to distinguish them?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are bile salt resistant, so that result never distinguishes among the species.
explanation.whyCorrect: All staphylococci grow in the presence of bile salts, so bile salt testing returns the same answer for every species and is useless for separating them. The useful discriminators are coagulase, hemolysis on blood agar, mannitol fermentation, and novobiocin sensitivity. This is why bile salt resistance appears as a uniform row across the identification table.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only S. aureus is beta-hemolytic; the other two are nonhemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only S. aureus produces coagulase, so this test separates it from the other two species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only S. aureus ferments mannitol, turning mannitol salt agar yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant; the other two are sensitive.

questions.stem: An isolate of Staphylococcus grows well both in an aerobic incubator and in an anaerobic jar. Which term best describes this organism's oxygen requirement?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are facultative anaerobes, capable of both aerobic and anaerobic growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Facultative anaerobes can generate energy with or without oxygen, which is exactly what all staphylococci do. This metabolic flexibility lets them grow on routine laboratory media under either atmosphere and colonize a wide range of body sites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aerotolerant anaerobe survives oxygen but cannot use it, whereas staphylococci grow aerobically.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A microaerophile requires reduced oxygen and grows poorly at atmospheric oxygen levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An obligate aerobe would fail to grow in the anaerobic jar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An obligate anaerobe would fail to grow in the aerobic incubator.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a warm, tender, rapidly spreading area of erythema on the shin that began at a small cut 2 days earlier. The process involves the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and there is no drainable collection of pus. Which term best describes this infection?

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is acute infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually starting at a break in the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cellulitis is an acute infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues that usually starts from a break in the skin caused by trauma or another infection. It is commonly caused by S. aureus and much less commonly by S. epidermidis. The inflammation is diffuse rather than walled off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abscess is a walled-off collection of pus, which is explicitly absent in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folliculitis is limited to a hair follicle and appears as a small tender pustule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impetigo is a superficial infection with honey-crusted lesions rather than deep spreading erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and would not be diagnosed from spreading skin erythema.

questions.stem: S. aureus produces an enzyme that causes blood clot formation. Which of the following best describes how this enzyme benefits the organism during infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds the Fc portion of IgG, inverting the antibody's orientation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cleaves the beta-lactam ring of penicillin, inactivating the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: It coats the organism in fibrin, shielding it from immune attack

choices.label: D
choices.text: It converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas

choices.label: E
choices.text: It forms pores in leukocyte membranes, killing those cells

explanation.summary: Coagulase builds an insoluble fibrin capsule that hides S. aureus from the immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coagulase causes blood clot formation, and a positive reaction creates an insoluble fibrin capsule around the microorganism. In vivo, that fibrin coat shields the pathogen from the immune response. In the laboratory the same enzyme clots plasma, which is a dead giveaway for S. aureus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That describes protein A, a surface protein that blocks opsonization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: That describes penicillinase, an antibiotic resistance enzyme rather than a clotting enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That describes catalase, which is produced by all staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That describes leukocidin, a pore-forming exotoxin that kills white blood cells.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has a purulent wound. Gram stain of the drainage shows gram-positive cocci. When a drop of hydrogen peroxide is added to a colony from the blood agar plate, no bubbling is observed. This test result is most useful for distinguishing the isolate from which of the following organisms?

explanation.summary: The catalase test separates catalase-negative streptococci and enterococci from catalase-positive staphylococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are gram-positive, nonmotile, non-spore-forming and uniformly catalase negative. Staphylococci produce catalase, which liberates oxygen bubbles from hydrogen peroxide. A negative catalase test therefore argues against Staphylococcus aureus and supports a streptococcal or enterococcal isolate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus species are also catalase negative, so the test cannot separate them from streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Streptococcus agalactiae is catalase negative and would also fail to bubble.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae is catalase negative and is not distinguished by this test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes is catalase negative and would give this same result.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-positive cocci arranged in pairs, with each coccus having a pointed, lancet-shaped end. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci are the classic morphology of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. pneumoniae is described as having a lancet-shaped appearance: the diplococci have a pointed end on each coccus. It is a leading cause of meningitis, and its capsule allows it to spread systemically and cross the blood-brain barrier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Staphylococcus aureus forms grape-like clusters, not pairs in chains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae appears in chains and is a neonatal rather than elderly meningitis pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mutans is a viridans streptococcus that appears in chains and causes dental caries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes appears in chains rather than as lancet-shaped pairs.

questions.stem: A throat swab from a 9-year-old with a sore throat is plated on blood agar. After overnight incubation the colonies are surrounded by a completely clear, transparent zone where the red blood cells have been destroyed. Gram stain shows cocci in chains. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Complete (beta) hemolysis on blood agar points to S. pyogenes or S. agalactiae; in a pharyngitis case it is S. pyogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are divided by how readily they lyse red blood cells. Beta hemolysis is complete destruction of RBCs, leaving a clear halo around the colony, and S. pyogenes and S. agalactiae are the beta-hemolytic species. S. pyogenes colonizes the skin and throat and is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus species are gamma-hemolytic (or alpha), leaving red blood cells intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. gallolyticus subspecies generally demonstrate gamma hemolysis (nonhemolytic).
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mitis is a viridans streptococcus and is alpha-hemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic aerobically, producing partial green discoloration rather than a clear zone.

questions.stem: Two beta-hemolytic streptococcal isolates are tested with a bacitracin disk. Isolate 1 shows a clear zone of inhibition around the disk; isolate 2 grows right up to the edge of the disk. Which of the following statements best interprets these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both isolates belong to Lancefield group B

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. agalactiae and isolate 2 is S. pyogenes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. pneumoniae and isolate 2 is S. mitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. pyogenes and isolate 2 is S. agalactiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither isolate can be assigned a Lancefield group

explanation.summary: Group A streptococci are bacitracin sensitive; group B streptococci are bacitracin resistant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacitracin is a polypeptide antibiotic that interferes with peptidoglycan synthesis. Group A streptococci such as S. pyogenes are inhibited by only a small amount of bacitracin, whereas group B streptococci such as S. agalactiae usually are not. The mnemonic B-BRAS captures this: group B strep are Resistant, group A strep are Sensitive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the bacitracin-resistant isolate fits group B; the sensitive one is group A.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the relationship; group B strep are the resistant organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. pneumoniae and S. mitis are alpha-hemolytic and are separated by optochin, not bacitracin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-hemolytic streptococci are precisely the group that is further classified by Lancefield grouping.

questions.stem: Sputum from a patient with lobar pneumonia grows an alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive coccus. Growth of the isolate is reliably inhibited around an optochin disk. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Optochin sensitivity separates S. pneumoniae from the other alpha-hemolytic streptococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: Optochin reliably inhibits the growth of S. pneumoniae on culture plates, while viridans and other streptococci are optochin resistant. S. pneumoniae is also the most common cause of bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which fits the clinical picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecium is gamma-hemolytic and is identified by growth in 6.5% NaCl.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae is beta-hemolytic and bacitracin resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mutans is a viridans streptococcus and is optochin resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic and is identified with the bacitracin disk.

questions.stem: An alpha-hemolytic gram-positive coccus is recovered from blood cultures. A turbid suspension of the organism is mixed with bile, and the turbidity clears. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The isolate belongs to Lancefield group A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The isolate is a viridans group streptococcus

choices.label: C
choices.text: The isolate is beta-hemolytic when grown aerobically

explanation.summary: Bile solubility distinguishes bile-soluble S. pneumoniae from the bile-insoluble viridans streptococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bile solubility test distinguishes bile-soluble S. pneumoniae from all other alpha-hemolytic (viridans) streptococci, which are bile insoluble. A clearing of the turbidity in the bile tube indicates a positive test, meaning the organism has lysed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lancefield grouping is applied to beta-hemolytic streptococci, not to this alpha-hemolytic isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viridans group streptococci are bile insoluble, so the tube would remain turbid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic in aerobic conditions and beta-hemolytic only anaerobically.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clearing of the tube defines a positive test, meaning the organism is bile soluble.

questions.stem: A reference laboratory types several beta-hemolytic streptococcal isolates using panels of specific antisera, assigning each isolate to a letter group. The serologic scheme these antisera rely on is based primarily on antigenic differences in which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzymatic hydrolysis of the PYR substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Susceptibility to optochin and to bacitracin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ability to grow in 6.5% sodium chloride

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hemolysins released onto blood agar

explanation.summary: Lancefield grouping is a serologic scheme based on surface antigens, chiefly cell wall carbohydrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are subdivided by antibodies that recognize surface antigens into Lancefield groups, which may include one or more species. Grouping is based on antigenic differences in cell wall carbohydrates (groups A to V), in cell wall pili-associated protein, and in the polysaccharide capsule in group B streptococci.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The PYR test is a biochemical assay for a specific enzyme, not an antigen-antibody reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Optochin and bacitracin susceptibility are physiologic tests, not serologic grouping.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salt tolerance is a biochemical test used to separate Enterococcus from nonenterococcal group D organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysin activity defines the alpha, beta, and gamma hemolytic patterns, a separate classification method.

questions.stem: A urine culture from a hospitalized 71-year-old man grows a catalase-negative, gamma-hemolytic gram-positive coccus. When the isolate is tested with the pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) reagent, the reagent turns cherry-red. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: A positive PYR test narrows a gram-positive coccus to S. pyogenes or Enterococcus; gamma hemolysis then points to Enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PYR test is used for presumptive identification of S. pyogenes and Enterococcus spp.; hydrolysis of the substrate turns the reagent pink or cherry-red. Since this isolate is gamma-hemolytic rather than beta-hemolytic, it is an Enterococcus, and enterococci commonly cause urinary tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae is beta-hemolytic and is not a PYR-positive organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. gallolyticus is gamma-hemolytic but is not identified by a positive PYR reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. mitis is an alpha-hemolytic viridans streptococcus of the oral cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and is identified by optochin sensitivity and bile solubility.

questions.stem: Two nonhemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive cocci are recovered from separate blood cultures. Both organisms grow in the presence of bile, but only isolate B also grows in broth containing 6.5% sodium chloride. Isolate B is best identified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Both group D strep and enterococci grow in bile, but only Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterococcus spp. are very similar to group D strep such as S. gallolyticus but can be distinguished by their ability to grow in salt. Both S. gallolyticus and Enterococcus spp. grow in bile, but only Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl media. E. faecalis and E. faecium are nonhemolytic and are the two named species.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S. gallolyticus grows in bile but does not tolerate 6.5% NaCl, matching isolate A instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mitis is an alpha-hemolytic viridans streptococcus, not a salt-tolerant nonhemolytic organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and bile soluble rather than nonhemolytic and salt tolerant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic and would not be described as nonhemolytic.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has 2 days of sore throat and malaise. Her temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), her pharynx is erythematous with enlarged tonsils, and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. She has no cough, rhinorrhea, or conjunctivitis. Which of the following features most strongly supports a bacterial rather than a viral cause of her pharyngitis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The absence of any measurable fever

explanation.summary: Fever plus cervical adenopathy without upper respiratory symptoms favors streptococcal pharyngitis over a viral cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. pyogenes is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis, and patients present with a combination of fever, malaise, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Viruses are by far the most common cause of pharyngitis overall, but they usually present without fever or adenopathy and with other respiratory symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjunctivitis is one of the upper respiratory findings that suggests a viral cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lower respiratory tract symptoms accompany viral pharyngitis rather than GAS infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rhinorrhea and cough are viral features rather than features of strep throat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lack of fever is characteristic of viral pharyngitis, not streptococcal disease.

questions.stem: A child with fever and a sore throat has a rapid strep test performed on a throat swab in clinic. A visible line appears within minutes, confirming the diagnosis. This point-of-care assay detects which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysin released onto a blood agar plate

explanation.summary: The rapid strep test is an antibody-based immunoassay for the group A carbohydrate antigen on a throat swab.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the clinic, the rapid antigen detection test for strep detects S. pyogenes by identifying the group-specific carbohydrate antigen in a throat swab using antibody-based immunoassay technology. A visible line indicates a positive result within minutes, which is very useful for confirming a diagnosis of strep throat.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Streptococci are catalase negative, so catalase activity is not the target of this assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysin activity is assessed by culture on blood agar, not by a swab-based strip test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-streptolysin O titers document a recent infection serologically, not an acute throat swab result.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rapid test described uses immunoassay technology rather than nucleic acid amplification.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has several crusted lesions on his chin and around his nose. The lesions are erythematous and covered with a honey-colored crust; no blisters are present. Nonbullous impetigo is diagnosed. Although S. pyogenes can produce these lesions, which of the following organisms is the most common cause of both nonbullous and bullous impetigo?

explanation.summary: Impetigo caused by S. pyogenes is nonbullous, but S. aureus is the most common cause of impetigo overall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impetigo is an epidermal skin infection producing crusted lesions at the site of inoculation, and impetigo caused by S. pyogenes is specifically nonbullous (nonblistering). Staphylococcus aureus, however, is the most common cause of both nonbullous and bullous impetigo.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococci cause endocarditis, urinary, biliary, and wound infections rather than impetigo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. agalactiae colonizes the vagina and GI tract and causes neonatal invasive disease, not impetigo.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. mutans is an oral organism that causes dental caries and subacute endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes respiratory and systemic infections rather than crusted skin lesions.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is taken to the operating room for a necrotizing infection of the thigh. Anaerobic culture of the debrided tissue grows rapidly overnight, and Gram stain of the isolate shows rods containing refractile terminal swellings. Which of the following best describes the genus to which this organism belongs?

explanation.summary: Clostridia are gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, spore-forming rods.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every clinically significant Clostridium species is a gram-positive, obligate anaerobic rod that forms endospores. The spores give the terminal swellings seen on Gram stain and allow the organism to survive oxygen exposure, heat, and drying. Rapid growth on anaerobic culture is also typical of the genus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clostridia stain gram-positive, not gram-negative, and they are obligate anaerobes rather than aerobes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clostridia are neither gram-negative nor aerobic, and they are true bacilli rather than coccobacilli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clostridia are rods (bacilli), not cocci, and they are gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clostridia are obligate anaerobes and they do form spores, so an aerobic non-spore-former does not fit.

questions.stem: A microbiology technologist performs motility testing on isolates of the five clinically significant Clostridia species. Four of the isolates are flagellated and motile, but one is consistently nonmotile. Which of the following is the nonmotile species?

explanation.summary: C. perfringens is the exception to the rule that Clostridia are flagellated and motile.
explanation.whyCorrect: With the exception of C. perfringens, Clostridia species are flagellated, motile organisms. C. perfringens lacks flagella and is nonmotile, which is a useful laboratory clue when an anaerobic gram-positive rod is recovered from a wound or from contaminated meat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. difficile is one of the motile Clostridia species.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. botulinum is flagellated and motile like most of the genus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C. septicum is motile; only C. perfringens is the stated exception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. tetani is among the flagellated, motile Clostridia.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man sustains a crush injury to the forearm in a farming accident. Tissue from the wound is plated on blood agar and incubated anaerobically. At 24 hours there are large, rapidly growing colonies, each surrounded by an inner zone of complete hemolysis and an outer zone of partial hemolysis. Which of the following organisms is most likely growing on this plate?

explanation.summary: A double zone of hemolysis on blood agar is the classic colony appearance of C. perfringens.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. perfringens produces a variety of toxins that, in addition to increasing virulence, generate a double ring of hemolysis around the colony on blood agar. Alpha toxin contributes to this pattern by perforating red blood cells. C. perfringens is also one of the two beta-hemolytic Clostridia and grows rapidly, matching the plate described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. difficile is gamma-hemolytic and does not lyse red blood cells, so no zone of hemolysis would appear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. botulinum is gamma-hemolytic and would leave the blood agar unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C. septicum is gamma-hemolytic and would not produce the double ring described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. tetani is beta-hemolytic but produces a single zone of hemolysis, not a double ring.

questions.stem: Gram stain of an anaerobic isolate recovered from a soil-contaminated wound shows slender bacilli, many with a terminal swelling that gives the cell a drumstick appearance. These structures are most directly responsible for which of the following properties?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attachment to colonic mucosa by surface pili

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fermentation of lactose on selective MacConkey agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of a thick polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance to detergents, heat, and desiccation

explanation.summary: The drumstick structures are endospores, which confer resistance to detergents, heat, and drying.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain Clostridia species are resistant to detergents, heat, and desiccation because they form endospores, and the spores of Clostridia have a characteristic drumstick appearance on stained smears. This durability is what allows Clostridia to survive adverse conditions, including the presence of oxygen, and to persist in soil and in hospital environments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adhesion to mucosa is a function of surface adhesins, not of the endospore, which is a dormant survival form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Spores have nothing to do with sugar fermentation, and MacConkey agar is a selective medium for gram-negative enteric organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endospores are structural survival forms and do not act enzymatically on complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A capsule is a separate surface structure; the drumstick appearance reflects an endospore within the cell.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhea on hospital day 9, six days after completing a course of antibiotics for pneumonia. The patient who occupied the same room the week before had an identical illness, and the room was cleaned between admissions. Which property of the responsible organism best explains this pattern of spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It forms biofilms on indwelling intravenous catheters

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forms endospores that resist detergents and drying

choices.label: C
choices.text: It grows only at temperatures above 42°C

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is transmitted by respiratory droplets over long distances

choices.label: E
choices.text: It survives within host macrophages for weeks

explanation.summary: C. difficile spores resist routine cleaning, which is why the organism spreads between hospitalized patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ability to form spores makes C. difficile very difficult to eliminate from hospitals, and spread from patient to patient across rooms is a major concern. The spores resist detergents, heat, and desiccation, so ordinary cleaning does not reliably remove them, and proper infection-control protocols are required to prevent transmission within a facility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catheter biofilm is not the mechanism; the reservoir here is spores on environmental surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth at high temperature is not a feature of C. difficile and would not explain environmental persistence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C. difficile spreads by the fecal-oral route from spores in stool, not by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. difficile causes toxin-mediated colitis at the mucosal surface rather than surviving as an intracellular pathogen.

questions.stem: An infection-control team screens stool specimens for asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile carriage in two groups: healthy community-dwelling adults and currently hospitalized inpatients. Which of the following pairs of carriage rates (healthy adults; hospitalized patients) is expected?

explanation.summary: C. difficile colonizes fewer than 5% of healthy adults but 20% to 50% of hospitalized patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. difficile may be found as normal intestinal flora, but colonization rates are relatively low in healthy adults at less than 5%. In contrast, colonization rates are high in hospitalized patients, in the range of 20% to 50%, because spores persist on hospital surfaces and antibiotic exposure clears the competing normal flora.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This underestimates inpatient carriage, which reaches 20% to 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This misses the marked increase in carriage that occurs with hospitalization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Healthy adults are colonized at well under 5%, not at 20% to 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rates are reversed; the high rate belongs to hospitalized patients, not healthy adults.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a patient with active Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, cleans her hands with an alcohol-based gel, and then cares for a second patient. Four days later the second patient develops malodorous watery diarrhea and tests positive for the same organism. Which of the following routes of transmission is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bloodborne spread from a contaminated intravenous line

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct inoculation of spores into broken skin on the hands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fecal-oral transfer of spores on hands and surfaces

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ingestion of preformed toxin present in hospital food

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhalation of aerosols from the ventilation system

explanation.summary: C. difficile is spread person to person by the fecal-oral route because spores are shed in feces.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. difficile may be spread from human to human by the fecal-oral route, as the spores can be found in feces. Coming into contact with surfaces contaminated with C. difficile-infected feces can spread the infection, and because the spores resist detergents and drying, hand and environmental contamination readily carries the organism from one patient to the next.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. difficile causes a toxin-mediated colitis rather than a line-associated bloodstream infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inoculation through broken skin describes how C. tetani and C. perfringens enter, not C. difficile.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C. difficile toxins are produced in the colon after the organism overgrows; disease does not follow ingestion of preformed toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. difficile is an enteric pathogen acquired by ingestion, not an airborne respiratory organism.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old farmer steps on a nail that penetrates his boot and drives soil deep into the plantar surface of his foot. Eight days later he develops jaw stiffness and painful spasms of the back muscles. Which feature of a deep puncture wound best explains why it favors the responsible organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It destroys circulating neutrophils throughout the extremity

choices.label: B
choices.text: It exposes the organism to high oxygen tension, triggering toxin release

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces the organism directly into the systemic circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides an anaerobic, nutrient-rich niche for spore germination

choices.label: E
choices.text: It raises local tissue pH, which activates bacterial proteases

explanation.summary: Puncture wounds create the anaerobic, nutrient-rich conditions C. tetani spores need to germinate.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. tetani is most commonly found in soil and can be inoculated into soft tissue following a puncture wound. Puncture wounds and trauma increase access to nutrients and provide an anaerobic environment for C. tetani spores to germinate and cause disease. Because C. tetani is an obligate anaerobe, this low-oxygen pocket is essential to converting dormant spores into toxin-producing bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutrophil destruction is not how a puncture wound promotes tetanus; the key factor is the anaerobic environment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxygen exposure is precisely what these obligate anaerobes avoid; spores stay dormant when oxygen is present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tetanus results from local germination and toxin production in the wound rather than from bloodstream inoculation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue pH is not the stated determinant; access to nutrients and low oxygen tension are.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of constipation and poor feeding. Her mother says the baby seems droopy and her sucking is weak. On further history, the mother reports that a relative advised her to put a sweet substance on her nipple to encourage the baby to feed. Which of the following is the most likely source of this infant's illness?

explanation.summary: Honey is the most common source of the C. botulinum spores that cause infant botulism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Honey is the most common source of the spores that transmit botulism to infants, which is why honey is avoided in children under 1 year of age. In infants under 2 years, ingested C. botulinum spores germinate in the immature bowel and produce toxin in situ, causing constipation followed by poor feeding, weak suck, and generalized hypotonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Home-canned foods such as green beans are a classic source of preformed toxin in adults rather than the usual source in infants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Soy-based formula is a recognized source of C. botulinum contamination but is not the most common source in infants, and it was not what this mother described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Undercooked meat transmits C. perfringens food poisoning, which causes watery diarrhea rather than hypotonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unpasteurized cider is not a described source of Clostridia and does not fit the sweet substance applied to the nipple.

questions.stem: At least 21 people who attended a church potluck dinner develop blurred vision, difficulty swallowing, and progressive weakness of the arms within 24 hours of the meal, and one 54-year-old woman dies. Investigators trace the illness to a potato salad prepared with home-canned potatoes. Which of the following is most likely responsible?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preformed botulinum toxin of C. botulinum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxins A and B of C. difficile

explanation.summary: Home-canned foods are a classic source of preformed botulinum toxin causing foodborne botulism in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. botulinum is associated with foodborne illness, and home-canned foods are a recognized source of contamination. In adults, botulism results from ingestion of preformed toxin rather than from spores. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing a descending paralysis that begins with the cranial nerves and causes blurred vision and dysphagia before limb weakness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha toxin causes myonecrosis and hemolysis in infected wounds, not a foodborne neurologic illness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. perfringens enterotoxin causes watery diarrhea within hours of eating meat, not cranial nerve palsies or paralysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetanospasmin causes spastic paralysis and lockjaw after wound inoculation, the opposite of a descending flaccid weakness after a meal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. difficile toxins act on the colon to produce diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, and follow antibiotic use rather than a shared meal.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old girl and her 6-year-old brother are both given honey by a caregiver. Two weeks later the infant is admitted with constipation, a weak cry, and generalized hypotonia, while her brother remains entirely well. Which of the following best explains why only the infant became ill?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The infant has a gastric pH too low to destroy the spores

choices.label: B
choices.text: The infant has a more permeable blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: The infant ingested a larger dose of toxin per kilogram

choices.label: D
choices.text: The infant lacks transplacental maternal antibody against the toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The infant's immature GI tract allows ingested spores to germinate

explanation.summary: Infants under 2 years are susceptible to botulism because their immature GI tract lets ingested spores germinate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infants younger than 2 years of age are especially susceptible because their GI tracts are immature and allow ingested spores to germinate in the bowel. In children older than 2 years the GI tract is more developed and can move the bacterial toxin through the gut before it has the opportunity to cause damage, so the older sibling is protected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low gastric pH would be protective; the stated mechanism is an immature gut that permits germination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Botulinum toxin acts peripherally at the neuromuscular junction, so blood-brain barrier permeability is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both children ingested the same food; the difference lies in whether spores can germinate, not in the dose received.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Susceptibility is explained by gut maturity and spore germination, not by the presence or absence of maternal antibody.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man develops abdominal cramping and profuse watery diarrhea 8 hours after eating reheated beef at a buffet. He has no fever and no vomiting, and his symptoms resolve completely the next day. Which of the following virulence factors is responsible for his illness?

explanation.summary: C. perfringens food poisoning is caused by a heat-labile enterotoxin acting on the intestinal epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to the toxins responsible for wound disease, C. perfringens possesses a heat-labile enterotoxin that acts on the intestinal epithelium and leads to profuse watery diarrhea. The illness follows ingestion of undercooked or contaminated meats, has an incubation period on the order of a few hours, and occurs without fever or emesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha toxin is the lecithinase responsible for myonecrosis and hemolysis in wound infection, not for foodborne diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Botulinum toxin causes descending flaccid paralysis, not cramping and watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetanospasmin is produced by C. tetani and causes spastic paralysis rather than gastrointestinal illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxin B is a C. difficile cytotoxin and produces antibiotic-associated colitis, not a few-hour foodborne illness.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is admitted with fever and confusion. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grows a facultative intracellular bacterium that tends to appear in clusters and pairs and that also grows well at 4°C. Gram stain of this isolate is most likely to show which of the following?

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive, facultative intracellular rod that grows in clusters and pairs and thrives at cold temperatures.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of facultative intracellular growth, a clustered and paired arrangement, and replication at refrigeration temperature identifies L. monocytogenes. On Gram stain the organism is a gram-positive rod. Its tendency to line up in clusters or pairs makes the arrangement superficially resemble Streptococcus, which is a classic reason it is misread on direct smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Branching, partially acid-fast filaments describe Nocardia, a filamentous organism with a completely different morphology from Listeria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative coccobacilli describe organisms such as Haemophilus; Listeria retains crystal violet and stains gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-negative diplococci describe Neisseria species, which are not facultative intracellular rods and do not grow at 4°C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram-positive cocci in clusters describes staphylococci; Listeria is a rod, even though its clustered arrangement can mimic a coccal pattern.

questions.stem: A public health laboratory is trying to recover a bacterial pathogen from refrigerated deli meat implicated in an outbreak. The specimen is held at 4°C (39.2°F) for a prolonged period before subculture, which allows the suspected organism to outgrow competing flora. This technique is most useful for isolating which of the following organisms?

explanation.summary: Cold enrichment at 4°C selectively recovers Listeria monocytogenes, which is unusual among bacteria in growing at refrigeration temperature.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike most bacteria, L. monocytogenes grows well in culture at temperatures as low as 4°C (39.2°F), a property exploited in the laboratory technique called cold enrichment. Holding a contaminated specimen in the cold suppresses other flora while Listeria continues to multiply. This same cold tolerance is why the organism persists in cooked, refrigerated foods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism requiring X and V factors at 35–37°C and does not replicate at refrigeration temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neisseria meningitidis is cold-sensitive and fastidious; specimens are kept warm rather than chilled to preserve viability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae grows optimally near body temperature and is not recovered by prolonged incubation in the cold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes requires enriched media near body temperature and would not outgrow competitors at 4°C.

questions.stem: An isolate from the blood of a 3-day-old newborn is streaked onto sheep blood agar perpendicular to a streak of Staphylococcus aureus. Where the two streaks converge, an area of enhanced, synergistic lysis of erythrocytes appears. Gram stain of the isolate shows gram-positive rods. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: A positive CAMP test in a gram-positive rod points to Listeria monocytogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. monocytogenes is CAMP test positive: its zone of hemolysis is enhanced when the organism is grown adjacent to S. aureus on blood agar, producing synergistic lysis of red blood cells. Combined with gram-positive rod morphology, this finding is characteristic of Listeria. It is one of the standard bench findings used to identify the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a gram-positive rod but is not beta-hemolytic and does not show CAMP synergy with S. aureus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterococcus faecalis is a gram-positive coccus, not a rod, and does not give the arrowhead pattern of enhanced hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a gram-positive coccus and is typically nonhemolytic on sheep blood agar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes is a gram-positive coccus that produces a wide zone of beta-hemolysis on its own, without synergy.

questions.stem: A gram-positive organism recovered from the cerebrospinal fluid of a 74-year-old man produces immediate vigorous bubbling when a colony is exposed to hydrogen peroxide. This single result argues most strongly against which of the following identifications?

explanation.summary: Listeria species are catalase positive, which separates them from the catalase-negative streptococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bubbling with hydrogen peroxide indicates catalase activity. Listeria spp. are catalase positive, as are staphylococci and corynebacteria. Streptococci, including S. agalactiae, are catalase negative, so a strongly positive catalase test excludes that identification. Catalase is therefore a useful first test when a gram-positive organism from CSF could be either Listeria or a streptococcus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is catalase positive, so a positive test does not argue against it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria monocytogenes is catalase positive, so a positive test is fully compatible with this organism rather than against it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcus aureus is catalase positive, so the result supports rather than excludes this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococcus epidermidis is also catalase positive and remains compatible with the result.

questions.stem: Sheep blood agar inoculated with cerebrospinal fluid from a 2-week-old infant grows small colonies of gram-positive rods. Each colony is surrounded by a clear zone that extends only slightly past the colony edge. Which of the following best describes this isolate's hemolytic pattern?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-hemolysis with green discoloration of the agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gamma-hemolysis with no change in the agar

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes is weakly beta-hemolytic, producing only a narrow zone of clearing on sheep blood agar.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeria spp. are weakly beta-hemolytic organisms that exhibit a narrow zone of hemolysis when grown on sheep's blood agar. The clearing is complete but subtle, extending just beyond the colony. This weak hemolysis is why the CAMP test, which enhances the zone next to S. aureus, is so helpful for identification.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A wide zone of beta-hemolysis is typical of S. pyogenes; Listeria hemolysis is described as weak and narrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-hemolysis produces partial lysis with a green discoloration and is characteristic of organisms such as S. pneumoniae, not Listeria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gamma-hemolysis means no lysis at all; Listeria does clear the agar, just over a narrow zone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Listeria hemolysis is readily seen under routine aerobic incubation and is not conditional on anaerobiosis.

questions.stem: A broth culture of a gram-positive rod is incubated at room temperature and examined as a wet mount. The bacteria show a characteristic end-over-end tumbling movement. Which of the following bacterial structures produces this form of motility?

explanation.summary: Outside the host cell at room temperature, Listeria monocytogenes shows flagella-driven tumbling motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeria spp. are flagellated, motile organisms. Outside of the cell at room temperature, L. monocytogenes is characterized by a classic tumbling motility in broth culture that is facilitated by its flagella. This extracellular tumbling is distinct from the organism's second, intracellular mode of movement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A capsule is a protective surface layer and contributes nothing to bacterial locomotion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A type III secretion apparatus injects effector proteins into host cells and does not propel the bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fimbriae mediate adherence to surfaces and do not generate the propulsive end-over-end movement seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerized host actin drives the organism's intracellular actin rockets, not the extracellular tumbling seen in broth.

questions.stem: Fluorescence microscopy of infected intestinal epithelial cells shows bacilli within the cytoplasm, each trailing a comet-shaped tail of rapidly polymerized host actin that propels the organism into adjacent cells. Which of the following bacterial products mediates this process?

explanation.summary: ActA is the Listeria protein that mediates intracellular motility by driving host actin polymerization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inside the host cell, L. monocytogenes forms actin rockets, using rapidly polymerized actin to move among and within host cells. ActA is the protein that mediates this intracellular motility via actin polymerization. This mechanism lets the organism spread cell to cell without re-entering the extracellular space, where antibodies could reach it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagellin forms the flagella responsible for extracellular tumbling motility, not intracellular actin-based propulsion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Internalin A is a surface protein that mediates adhesion to and invasion of enterocytes, a step that precedes cytoplasmic movement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Listeriolysin O disrupts the phagosomal membrane so the organism escapes into the cytosol; it does not build actin tails.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phospholipase C also works on host membranes to allow phagosomal escape rather than driving actin polymerization.

questions.stem: After being taken up by a macrophage through phagocytosis, Listeria monocytogenes escapes into the cytosol rather than being digested. Which of the following bacterial products is most directly responsible for this escape?

explanation.summary: Listeriolysin O lets Listeria avoid digestion in the phagosome by disrupting the host membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeriolysin O helps the bacterium avoid digestion in phagosomes after host cell entry via phagocytosis. Its mechanism is host cell membrane disruption, which is also why the organism lyses erythrocytes and appears hemolytic on blood agar. Escaping into the cytosol is the step that permits the organism to survive as a facultative intracellular pathogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ActA mediates intracellular movement through actin polymerization only after the organism has already reached the cytosol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase is a metabolic enzyme used for laboratory identification and is not the factor described as mediating phagosomal escape.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flagellin builds flagella for extracellular tumbling motility and has no role in breaching the phagosomal membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Internalin A mediates attachment to and invasion of host cells, a step that occurs before the organism is inside a phagosome.

questions.stem: A mutant strain of Listeria monocytogenes is constructed in the laboratory. When macrophages are infected with it, the bacteria remain confined within phagosomes and are degraded. Loss of which of the following pairs of products best explains this phenotype?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Internalin A and internalin B proteins

explanation.summary: Listeriolysin O and phospholipase C together allow Listeria to break out of the phagosome after being ingested.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeriolysin O and phospholipase C enzymes help the bacteria avoid digestion in phagosomes following host cell entry via phagocytosis. Both act by disrupting host cell membranes. A mutant lacking both would be taken up normally but would be trapped and destroyed inside the phagosome, exactly the phenotype described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ActA and flagellin govern movement inside and outside the cell; their loss would impair spread but would not trap the organism in a phagosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase and superoxide dismutase are not the factors this brick identifies as mediating phagosomal escape in Listeria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulase and protein A are staphylococcal products and are not produced by Listeria monocytogenes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Internalins mediate adhesion and invasion, so their loss would reduce entry into host cells rather than block escape after uptake.

questions.stem: After contaminated food is swallowed, Listeria monocytogenes must attach to and invade the enterocytes lining the gastrointestinal epithelium before it can reach the circulation. Which of the following bacterial surface proteins mediates this adhesion and invasion step?

explanation.summary: Internalin surface proteins mediate Listeria adhesion to and invasion of host cells, including enterocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Internalins are the surface proteins that allow L. monocytogenes to adhere to and invade the GI epithelium. Internalin A targets enterocytes, while internalin B targets endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and enterocytes. This invasion of the gut lining is the second step in the pathway from ingestion of contaminated food to dissemination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ActA drives propulsion through the cytosol by actin polymerization after the organism is already inside a cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagellin builds the flagella responsible for extracellular tumbling motility and does not mediate host cell invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Listeriolysin O disrupts the phagosomal membrane after uptake rather than mediating initial attachment to enterocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phospholipase C also acts on host membranes to permit phagosomal escape and is not an adhesion protein.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man has a 1-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He has vomited four times today. He recently visited his son's farm, where he drank several glasses of fresh milk taken directly from the farm's supply. Examination shows mild generalized abdominal tenderness. There is no blood in the stool. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Unpasteurized dairy is a classic vehicle for Listeria monocytogenes, which pasteurization would otherwise kill.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common route of transmission for L. monocytogenes is ingestion of contaminated food, and unpasteurized dairy products are a leading source. Routine pasteurization at commercial dairies kills the organism, so fresh farm milk that has not been pasteurized is the exposure that stands out here. In an older adult the resulting illness can be more severe than the mild gastroenteritis seen in healthy adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacillus cereus food poisoning is classically linked to reheated fried rice, not to unpasteurized milk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clostridioides difficile colitis follows antibiotic exposure with disruption of colonic flora, which this patient does not report.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norovirus spreads person to person or through contaminated shared food and would not be specifically tied to raw farm milk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vibrio parahaemolyticus gastroenteritis follows ingestion of raw or undercooked seafood rather than dairy.

questions.stem: A microbiologist preparing an environmental sampling plan asks where Listeria monocytogenes is most commonly found outside of infected patients. Which of the following best describes the organism's natural distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arthropod vectors such as ticks, fleas, and mosquitoes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospital water systems and air-conditioning cooling towers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Soil, water, plant life, and the feces of animal carriers

choices.label: D
choices.text: The human nasopharynx, with no environmental reservoir

choices.label: E
choices.text: The intestinal tract of shellfish and other marine animals

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes is abundant in the general environment and in animal carriers, including humans.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. monocytogenes is abundant in the environment and can be found in plant life, soil, water, and animal carriers, including humans. It can also be isolated from animal feces, and humans may carry a low level of the organism as gastrointestinal flora. This wide environmental distribution explains how the organism repeatedly enters the food supply.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Listeria is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food or vertically, not through arthropod vectors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Water systems and cooling towers are the reservoir for Legionella, not for Listeria monocytogenes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Listeria is not a nasopharyngeal colonizer, and it has an extensive environmental reservoir in soil, water, and plants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shellfish are not the defining reservoir; the organism is widespread in terrestrial environments and farm animals.
